one_liner: Pure safe-Rust WebP codec (image-webp fork): lossless encode 1.6-2.8x faster than libwebp m4, decode faster than FFmpeg.
what_it_does: A fork of image-rs/image-webp 0.2.4 that decodes VP8 (lossy), VP8L (lossless), alpha and animated WebP, and encodes lossless VP8L only. The API is image-webp's: WebPDecoder::new(reader) with read_image() for RGB(A), read_frame() for animation, or read_yuv420() for zero-copy BT.601 4:2:0 planes from still lossy files; WebPEncoder::new(writer).encode(pixels, w, h, ColorType), with EncoderParams to fall back to the old runs-only encoder. It lives as crates/rusty_webp in the remade_ffmpeg_rs monorepo, where the rff-codec-webp adapter puts it behind the ffmpeg-style rff CLI. It does not replace libwebp's C API.
how_it_is_fast: The encoder searches far less than libwebp at m4. It uses greedy hash-chain LZ77 over the ARGB pixels (32 candidates per position, cut to 8 and then 2 in long matchless stretches, an early exit at 128-pixel matches, and an unconditional distance-1 probe). It codes one Huffman group for the whole image, with no entropy image or histogram clustering. The color-cache size is picked from 0, 4, 6, 8 or 10 bits by a Shannon estimate. Per 16x16 tile it picks one of the 14 predictors by summed wrap-around residual magnitude, and the only other transform is subtract-green. A sampling dispatch skips the per-tile search on large run-heavy images. The decoder's speed-ups over upstream are a branch-free i16 select formulation of the normal loop filter, run over whole 16-lane (luma) or 8-lane (chroma) edges so the compiler can auto-vectorize it (no intrinsics), a block-scoped FastSession in the boolean decoder (one state snapshot and one validity check per coefficient block), a DC-only IDCT path, and native YUV output that skips RGB conversion.
when_to_use: You must emit lossless WebP from pure Rust with no C, no FFI and #![forbid(unsafe_code)], and encode time matters more than the last 4-13% of file size on photographs.
Screen captures, UI and other repeated content, where the first-party corpus shows files up to 39% smaller than libwebp m4.

Video or YUV pipelines that ingest still lossy WebP: read_yuv420() returns the native 4:2:0 planes zero-copy, and the authors report bit-exact output against FFmpeg's decoder (webp to y4m) on their corpus.
Decoding animated WebP in Rust into composited canvas frames with per-frame durations (FFmpeg's native webp decoder errors on these files).
You use upstream image-webp and want better lossless compression: upstream's runs-only encoder was 35-53% larger than libwebp on photos, per this fork's NOTICE.md.
when_not_to_use: Lossy WebP encoding. There is no VP8 encoder, and animation encoding is not supported either.

Smallest lossless files. libwebp m4 is 4-13% smaller on photos. The encoder has no color-indexing (palette) transform, no cross-color transform and no entropy image, so low-colour graphics could fall further behind (an inference; the corpus results are given only as ranges).

You need to know how it compares with libwebp's decoder (dwebp). That was never measured: the decode baseline is FFmpeg's native VP8/VP8L decoder. Upstream image-webp puts its own decoding at 70-100% of libwebp, and before this fork's speed work it was 1.18x slower than FFmpeg on the 8K lossy test.

Lossless encoding of very large images on tight memory. Reading the code gives a peak of about 30 bytes per pixel (RGBA copy, residual copy, u32 pixel array, hash-chain links and a 12-byte token per pixel), which is about 1 GB for a 7680x4320 frame. This was derived from the code, not measured.

You need maturity or outside validation. It is one crate in a 6-star monorepo with two commits (both 2026-08-12) and 1,025 crates.io downloads, against 83 million for upstream image-webp. No numbers have been measured by anyone other than the authors.

integration.form: crate (rusty_webp 0.1.1 on crates.io; source in crates/rusty_webp of remade_ffmpeg_rs)
integration.dependencies: byteorder-lite 0.1, quick-error 2.0.1; dev only: rand 0.8, rusty_alloc-api (the house allocator used by the example bench)
integration.min_toolchain: Declared rust-version 1.80.1 (inherited from upstream), but encoder.rs calls Option::is_none_or, which became stable in Rust 1.82, so 1.82+ is needed in practice. Edition 2021; the workspace pins 1.95.0.
integration.platforms: any Rust target: safe code only, with no arch-specific SIMD (the speed relies on auto-vectorization)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Decoder and encoder are single-threaded owned values, and no global mutable state was found in the crate (the opt-in profile feature only prints timings to stderr).

gotchas: The MSRV is wrong. Cargo.toml says 1.80.1, but the encoder's cache-size selection uses Option::is_none_or (stable since 1.82), so builds on 1.80 or 1.81 fail.

The bit-exactness claim covers the YUV path only (webp to y4m against FFmpeg). RGB output goes through fancy bilinear upsampling with libwebp's fixed-point constants and was not reported as compared against dwebp. The rff CLI switches to that path only when RFF_WEBP_UPSAMPLE is set.

Only the normal loop filter received the batched 16-lane kernels. Files encoded with VP8's simple loop filter still run the scalar per-pixel edge functions, so the decode speed-up may not carry over to them.

Encoder behaviour depends on content. Images over 262,144 pixels where at least 25% of sampled pixels repeat their left neighbour get one fixed 'top' predictor for the whole image instead of the per-tile search. Below that size the 14-way search always runs, at about 14 predictor evaluations per pixel.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when the output has to be WebP and the program has to be pure safe Rust. nativewebp is the Go analogue (a pure-Go lossless WebP encoder), @napi-rs/image drives libwebp itself from Node, and libjxl's fjxl, fpnge or QOI/QOIR encode far faster when you are free to choose a different format.
verified_claims_summary: First-party only, against FFmpeg 8.1.2 on one pinned core with ABBA-interleaved pairs and child CPU time. Lossless VP8L encode (N=21, per the commit message) ran 1.6-2.8x faster than ffmpeg -c:v libwebp -lossless 1 at the default effort m4. Photo files came out 4-13% larger (but smaller than m0), and screen content up to 39% smaller. An 8K lossy decode test (N=31, two runs) ran 1.24-1.29x faster than FFmpeg's native VP8 decoder with bit-exact YUV output, and 8K lossless decode ran about 2.15x faster than FFmpeg's native VP8L decoder. CPU, OS, rustc flags, corpus files and the WebP harness are not published.
status_note: The monorepo is active (506 commits, latest 2026-10-05), but the rusty_webp crate has not changed since it was created on 2026-08-12. The crate is MIT OR Apache-2.0, safe code with two small dependencies, and about 9.6k lines, so it is easy to vendor. The first-party numbers have no published harness to reproduce them.
measurement_notes: For the orchestrator. No correctness bug was found behind the numbers. The encoder's VP8L stream writing was checked against the spec: transform order, the 14 predictors including Select and ClampAddSubtractHalf, the rightmost-column TR rule, color-cache hashing and the length/distance prefix codes. The batched loop-filter kernels were checked against RFC 6386 15.3. The commit message also says FFmpeg decodes every encoded file bit-exact to the source. The harness has these weaknesses. (1) The WebP harness is still unpublished. Commit 26cad51 (2026-08-12) carries the numbers only in its message, and neither committed harness fits it: pinab.py needs each arm to print 'total <ms> ms', which ffmpeg does not do, and codec-bench.ps1 (first committed 2026-09-06) is HEVC-oriented with a frame-count parity check. (2) The README's 'null-arm floor <= 5%' is, in this project's harnesses, the reference timed against itself, so it is a noise floor and not a bound on overhead. Child CPU time includes process launch, demux and, for encode, input decoding plus ffmpeg's conversion to the RGB32 that the libwebp wrapper takes. Those costs differ between the ffmpeg and rff binaries. (3) The README measured child CPU time. The project's own later codec-bench.ps1 warns that Windows TotalProcessorTime is a 15.625 ms tick lattice that produced phantom published differences, and moved to a QPC wall clock. The tooling is Windows-oriented (PowerShell, .exe arms, psutil HIGH_PRIORITY_CLASS), so the WebP rows may share that resolution problem. The OS is not stated. (4) Per the commit message, the lossy-decode 1.24-1.29x is one '8K lossy' test with two confirming N=31 runs. The range is run-to-run spread, not a spread across corpus images. The lossless-decode 2.15x has no N or file stated. (5) Encode speed is compared only against libwebp m4. Since the photo sizes fall between m0 and m4, the missing comparison is libwebp m1-m3 speed at matched size. Other findings: declared rust-version 1.80.1, but Option::is_none_or (Rust 1.82) is used in encoder.rs; the simple loop filter is not batched; the encode peak is about 30 bytes per pixel, derived from the code. No new seed leads: fast-webp wraps libwebp, and zenwebp is already rejected.
